messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Last spring, we did a helicopter aerial survey of a small caribou population using distance sampling. The Torngat Mountains caribou Herd range extends north of the tree line over northeastern Quebec and Labrador (Canada) between 58 and 60.5 N. This herd is susceptible to be soon designated at risk in Canada. The tundra habitat, snow cover and type of aircraft all provided excellent visibility during the survey. Following an extensive survey effort on 98 transects (about 82% of the traditional range was covered), a total of 58 caribou groups (from 1 to 38 caribou, means= 10.5) were detected up to 2000 metres on both sides of the helicopter. Perpendicular distances were accurately measured using overhead GPS fixes taken while flying off transect to the initial location where the caribou groups were first detected (based on tracks in the snow). Later, during the analysis in Distance 7.1, we right-truncated at 1390 metres, removing 2 groups (3.4% of the small dataset) for final analysis. Model fit was good with the truncated dataset and herd size was estimated using best and parsimonious model CDS HN Cos(0) at 1326 caribou (CV= 0.257).

During exploratory analysis, we investigated relationship between group size and perpendicular distance from transects. This relationship is shown in the figure below. During preparation of the draft report, we wrote that “Regression of group size (y) as a function of perpendicular distance (x) suggests that any such relationship was very weak and non-significant (p= 0.013, r2= 0.047, Figure 5)”. One report reviewer disagreed with this statement and suggested that there was some relationship between Group size and Distance which could invalidate or modify data analysis in Distance 7.1 (i.e., having to include cluster size as a covariate).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-EIBQ4asHUpk/WiCznyf1EgI/AAAAAAAAAAM/gp8anWmaKkEhybxuD4QvIRGS5tc_E2uzgCLcBGAs/s1600/Caribou_survey_Figure_5.jpg>

The study description was long, but my question is simple. Is there any rule of thumb to guide researcher decision when investigating group size effect on perpendicular distance?

Thanks for your help.

Serge

messages.body_plain:
Dear Serge and List,

It's a bit hard to tell from the plot you show whether there might be a
"size bias" issue.  The default option in Distance is to do a regression
of log(cluster size) against estimated probability of detection -- the
log is applied to cluster size because it tends to be right skewed with
a few big clusters, and the prob of detection is because it's decreasing
prob of detection that causes size bias, rather than distance per se.
This is described in detail in Section 3.5.4 of the Introduction to
Distance Sampling book (Buckland et al. 2001).  The effect of the log
transform will be to squash the top part of your y-axis, and the effect
of using estimated prob of detection rather than distance will be to
contract the right hand side of your x-axis (as well as flip the plot
round - it's the intercept at estimated prob of detection 1 that is used
as the size bias-corrected estimate of group size).

Back in days gone by, Distance used to do a statistical test on the
slope of that regression, and would use the size-bias method if p<=0.15;
otherwise it would use the straight average.  (A p-value of 0.15 comes
from an equivalence between using that value and AIC-based model
selection in this case.)  But for about the past 15 years the default
has been just to apply the size bias regression estimate no matter what
the p-value.  Experience has shown that the intercept of the regression
is not much (if any) less precise than the straight mean cluster size,
and the problem with hypothesis tests is that they don't just test the
biological significance of a relationship, but also the sample size.

You do have a suspicious absence of small group sizes at bigger
distances (corresponding with smaller prob of detection) so the size
bias regression might well produce a statistically significant slope on
your data.  Even if not, if you want to follow standard practice from
conventional distance sampling, just use the size bias method that's the
default in Distance.

Another more modern alternative is to try cluster size as a covariate in
the detection function, using Multiple Covariate Distance Sampling, and
use AIC to decide whether to include it or not.

I hope this helps, Len

P.S. Regarding your CV, it's not bad considering only about 60 groups
seen, but just to double check: I assume the biggest contributor to the
variance was variation in encounter rate?  Were you able to pre-stratify
the survey into high and low density areas?  Did you do a systematic
survey and, if so, are you using one of the systematic survey variance
estimators (in Distance, Model Definition, under Properties, Variance,
Advanced, S2 or probably better O2.)  I'm happy to correspond with you
off the list on these issues if it would be helpful.

--

Serge, adding to Len’s comments, perhaps the problem that the reviewer identified is that your statement is incorrect:

‘During preparation of the draft report, we wrote that “Regression of group size (y) as a function of perpendicular distance (x) suggests that any such relationship was very weak and non-significant (p= 0.013, r2= 0.047, Figure 5)”.’

If the p-value was 0.013, then it would only be ‘non-significant’ if you were testing at the 1% level or more.  It is significant at the 5% level.  As Len says, you lose nothing by correcting for size-bias – even if it’s not there – so, given any uncertainty over whether there is size-bias, why not do so?

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hi Serge,

Yes, indeed, if you used the size bias method that's the default in
Distance then it will have dealt with the size bias effect.  I see from
the table you attached that the p-value on the size bias regression of
ln(cluster size) vs estimated detection prob is 0.013, so significant at
the 0.05 level.  However, significant or not, the default in Distance is
to use the size bias regression intercept (the Expected cluster size in
your table), in this case 8.63 with SE 1.29, so about 15% smaller than
the mean cluster size.

You might want to revise your report to clarify that the size bias
regression was used, and to qualify or remove the part where you say
there is no size bias effect -- the regression of cluster size against
distance is not really so informative in this regard.

Yes, I think you don't need to worry about cluster size as a covariate.

Cheers, Len

Thanks for clarifying Serge.  Whatever the p-value, you cannot conclude that ‘there is no group size effect on distance’.  The fact that you can’t reject a null hypothesis does not prove that the hypothesis is true – and when sample size is small, quite large size bias might well result in data that show no significant effect.  So in my view, safer to make the adjustment as there is little if any loss from doing so.

The MCDS approach is less ad hoc, and may prove to be better, but the default method in Distance should do an adequate job of correcting for any size bias.  So no need in my view to go to mcds.  But such an analysis is easy to do, so no harm in trying it.

Steve

Pierre

Hello Pierre and List:

We have used strut markers on fixed-wing aerial surveys for Distance Sampling of pronghorn in Wyoming for quite some time. I will share with you our experiences and some comments.  There are certainly many sources for measurement error in aerial surveys and we try to recognize, minimize and correct for them when we can. However, I haven't found a perfect technique. Please excuse the length of my responses but I hope it helps clarify issues.

First, I want to state that I am a biologist and not a pilot or aircraft mechanic. However I will share with you what I have been told or seen put in operation in our surveys over >25 years with a variety of fixed-wing aircraft, including Cessnas, Maules, SuperCubs, Terns, Huskies, Scouts and the like using a variety of flight services.  I have not set up any planes for a while so some of what I offer may or may not hold. Perhaps it will help guide you to the right answers. The first consideration to any aerial survey is safety.

Second, I want to clarify that any distance marking system using calibrated strut markers depends on several factors:
(a) that the markers are based upon a set eye position (not a mark on a window but the actual eye position when assigning clusters to distance intervals);
(b) that you need to align 2 specific strut marks with 2 window marks to get the observer's eye in the specified position to assign observations to perpendicular distances with this type of system (I have a PPT from the 2013 TWS Conference I can share that illustrates this);
(c) that the strut markers are set-up for a known height above ground level (AGL); and
(d) that (at least in terrestrial surveys) you need to measure the height AGL in order to correct the prescribed ground distance intervals for which the struts were marked to the actual intervals delineated by the strut markers for each sighting during the survey (Wyoming used laser rangefinders and digital radar altimeters to get AGLs which were recorded along with GPS and other data electronically).

Using marks on struts without these other measures has tremendous potential for measurement inaccuracies. I do not recommend using strut markers alone. You really need to specify an eye position, provide a means for observers to get their eye in that specified position when assigning observations to ground distance bands; and record the actual AGL to correct for deviations from the planned survey AGL.

Given these qualifications, the next question relates to the attachment of dowels to struts and their airworthiness.  The interpretation that we have been given by FAA Field Inspectors in our region of the USA (as told to me through our pilots) is that we generally did not need an FAA 337 Airworthiness Certificate to attach strut markers and other things like laser rangefinders and telemetry antennas as long as they were non-permanent and relatively light weight and aerodynamic. That did mean we operated in a Restricted Category: only essential crew would be on the flight.  Some of the flight services we hired do have more permanent mounts for their plane and I understand the 337 Certificate is needed in at least some of those instances. And yes, I understand that the 337 application needs to include engineering drawings, testing data and other specifications and can be expensive. If a 337 certificate exists for the device you want to put on the plane then I understand you don't have to resubmit an application for that device, just reference it. Most of the aircraft systems we have used to attach strut markers have not required a 337 because they are not-permanently attached and pretty minor.  Your pilot might want to check with FAA Field Inspectors (or comparable regulatory agencies) in your area and other pilots conducting similarly set-up surveys (I can give you some references for flight services used by Wyoming off-list if you like). Again, things need to be safe and secure in flight.

We have used a variety of systems to attach dowels to struts, including variations on hose clamps, plastic zip ties, velcro on certain types of struts, and custom made brackets that attach via hose clamps to the strut.

You asked about ribbons or cords to mark distance bands on struts. My experience with these approaches has been that the trailing ends and most of the cords whip around a lot, except for a very short distance from the trailing edge of the strut. You have to visually extrapolate the "mid-line" to have a straight reference. If you use more than 1 cord on a strut to mark distance intervals then the potential is there for the ends to interfere with each other while they are whipping around.  I have not found strings, cords, or ribbons to work very well (I tried them during my MS research on pronghorn back in the Dark Ages). Another drawback of using ribbons etc. is that we find it helpful for markers to extend ahead of the strut a ways, especially for observers sitting in front seats, and non-rigid materials don't allow for that.

One of the concerns relative to using multiple stems/dowels/sticks/rods etc. to mark several intervals on each strut is that the innermost markers may make it difficult to get in and out of the door without bumping the dowels and possibly getting them out of alignment.  One of the approaches we have used to address this problem is to use retractable auto antenna blanks (available from most automotive supply stores), preferably in black. We cut the base off with bolt cutters and attach them to struts similarly to rigid dowels.  They can be retracted when not flying a survey. Depending upon the type of aircraft, you either reached under the door or through a window to extend or retract them. In Wyoming, many of our planes used for distance sampling were also used for telemetry and other surveys. Our pilots usually left the strut markers on the plane throughout the pronghorn abundance survey season. Another thing we do now is attach the rod over the strut as opposed to hanging it underneath. That allows the observer to have a continuous boundary between distance intervals.

Finally, you asked about alternatives to the type of strut marker system we've been discussing. For terrestrial fixed-wing surveys over varying terrain, there are not many options. A lot depends upon the density of clusters in the area you are sampling (i.e., encounter rate), the survey height AGL, and how precisely you can navigate your transect. In a number of aerial surveys using helicopters in relatively low density populations, distances are obtained via GPS positions perpendicular to the line by flying off-line to that point. I don't think that approach is particularly good for fixed-wing surveys, at least for pronghorn in the densities I have experienced.

Another approach that has been used with aerial surveys of some marine mammals is to obtain distances using an inclinometer marked on the window to get angles at known heights AGL. I have personally never used this approach (I'm sure others on the list have).. I understand this requires one of the horizontal marks to be aligned with the horizon (presumed to be essentially at infinity distance) and then the angle is measured downward and later converted to a perpendicular distance. I don't think this would be particularly viable for most terrestrial surveys because most landscapes are variable such that the distance to the horizon varies as well as the survey height AGL. However,  Nielsen et al. (Nielson, R. M., L. L. McDonald, and S.D. Kovach. 2006. Aerial line transect survey protocols and data analysis methods to monitor moose (Alces alces) abundance as applied on the Innoko National Wildlife Refuge, Alaska. Technical report prepared for US Fish and Wildlife Service, McGrath, Alaska, USA.) described a system for marking arcs on the windows of a helicopter for moose surveys in Alaska, but I doubt it would be viable for most fixed-wing surveys. I believe that most of those marine mammal surveys rely on flying a constant height AGL (which is more likely to happen when flying over the open ocean and relying on pressure altitude readings). See also Marques et al. 2006. Wildlife Society Bulletin 34(3):759-763. Southwell et al. (2002. Wildlife Society Bulletin 30:394-404) described an automated system to record distance sightings from a helicopter. To my knowledge, that type of system was custom-built and has not been applied elsewhere

I hope this has been helpful. Please feel free to contact me directly if you have further questions.

Good luck,

Rich Guenzel
Wyoming Game & Fish Dept. (retired)
Laramie, WY
USA

Hello,

I have flown mainly marine mammal surveys and we have always used an inclinometer to declination, which is translated into distance as the altitude is known. The most common one we have used is the Suunto like the one shown here https://www.amazon.com/Suunto-PM-5-Compass/dp/B003C02IWI

In recent surveys we have used a device called a Geometer which is described here http://geometer.pitemp.com/the-geometer-p1/ It records declination angles, time and gps data directly to a text file, and for us at least is easier for observers to use and provides more accurate measurements. It is also faster to use than the analogue inclinometers which is important in high density patches.

Usually we take measurements as the sighting passes abeam of the aircraft but it is possible to take them at any point if the lateral angle can be estimated. However the present version of the geometer does not yet measure lateral angles (i.e. angle from the nose of the aircraft) accurately enough.

I have never used strut markers and I struggle to think of a circumstance when we would. Do you use them because you are encountering very high densities, giving the observer insufficient time to use a device? That can indeed be a problem when using an analogue inclinometer, although the Geometer is much better in this respect.

Hope you find a solution to your issues.

Best regards,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Nicolás

As you know, using model-based methods of inference of density surface modelling does not provide you with the ability to use formulas for approximate amount of effort needed to achieve desired levels of precision as in section 2.4 of Buckland et al. (2015).

Nevertheless, you still need to estimate the parameters of the detection function best for your sightings--so advice in Section 2.4.1 about 60-80 sightings to estimate those parameters well still holds.  It is possible to estimate detection function parameters with fewer sightings, but reliability of that endeavour is more down to luck.  With small numbers of detections, inclusion/exclusion of a couple of detections near the transect may have profound consequences for the shape of the estimated detection function -- and consequently the estimated number of animals in the non-empty segments.

To produce reliable inference from your model-based estimates from data in your 81 segments is harder to judge.  The quality of this inference depends upon the proportion of those segments where there were detections as well as the quality of the explanatory model fitted--which is contingent upon the predictor variables used and their explanatory power.

Sorry the answer is vague, but that is the nature of sample size determination with model-based inference.

messages.body_plain:
Ana

The trick is for detections without distances, you provide a fictitious distance.  However, you do not want this fictitious distance to be used in the fitting of the detection function (hence use the data filter with a criterion that specifies certain detections--with fictitious distances) are not to be used in the analysis.

You then perform a second analysis of the data, this time without the filter such that all data are included in the analysis, but detection probability is provided as a multiplier, and not computed in this second analysis (you specify a uniform key with no adjustments).

Note the additional caveats in this users guide description:

"Note an important assumption here is that the missing distances are missing at random – for example it will not work if you are less likely to record the distance for objects farther from the line or point.  For this reason, the first approach is probably safer.  Note also that this approach won’t work if you use stratification – in that case you’ll need more than one multiplier (one for each stratum), and will have to calculate the global density estimate by hand. "

The advice is to discard observations with missing distances unless there are exceptional circumstances.

Carolin

This may get you a part of your answer.

Given that your data structure is such that you have transects within strata (indicated via sample.label and region.label variables), ds() has likely produced the point estimates you desire.

I use the "tee data" provided and used in the example for the ds() function:
library(Distance)
data(book.tee.data)
tee.data<-book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe[book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe$observer==1,]
region <- book.tee.data$book.tee.region
samples <- book.tee.data$book.tee.samples
obs <- book.tee.data$book.tee.obs
ds.dht.model <- ds(tee.data,4,region.table=region,
                   sample.table=samples,obs.table=obs)
str(ds.dht.model$dht$individuals$bysample)

you will find that the object created by ds() (when region, sample and observation tables are provide) contains sample-specific point estimates of density and abundance.

Your challenge would be to produce measures of precision for those estimates; using the delta method.

I haven't closely read the paper by Acevedo et al. to know if they produced the figure you show at the sample-level or region-level; the paper describes them as "site" estimates.

It may very well be the case that there is great uncertainty in your estimates of lizard density and a CV of 30% is the best that can be achieved under the design you implemented. Carolin

No, I meant approximation of variance approach called the delta method.  The calculation of the transect-level estimate is described in the function dht() as a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator using estimated values of detection probability for each detection to scale-up the count to an estimate of abundance.

"Abundance is estimated with a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator (Huggins 1989, 1991; Borchers et al 1998; Borchers and Burnham 2004). The abundance in the sampled region is simply 1/p_1 + 1/p_2 + ... + 1/p_nwhere p_i is the estimated detection probability for the ith detection of n total observations. It is not strictly a Horvitz-Thompson estimator because the p_i are estimated and not known. For animals observed in tight clusters, that estimator gives the abundance of groups (group=TRUE in options) and the abundance of individuals is estimated as s_1/p_1 + s_2/p_2 + ... + s_n/p_n, where s_i is the size (e.g., number of animals in the group) of each observation (group=FALSE in options)."
Calculation of precision for these point estimates should involve a) uncertainty in detection probability (derived from uncertainty in parameter estimates in your detection function -- that has several covariates as I recall) and b) uncertainty in the encounter rate.  However, your design has no uncertainty in encounter rate because you have no replicates at the sample level.  I suspect the software opts not to present a measure of precision based solely upon the uncertainty in the parameter estimates.  To my knowledge, those would be quite difficult calculations to carry out.

With regard to your second question of which of the cutpoint histograms to present.  Given a choice between the two you present, I would suggest you present the 20m cutpoints.  Keep in mind there is no requirement that the cutpoints be of equal width throughout the range of perpendicular distances.  With the 20m graph, you are better able to discuss the potential challenges in the data apparent in the first two bins.  This subtlety of the data is not apparent with the 30m histograms.

Brigham Whitman

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Is there a standard method for comparing encounter rates?
messages.body_plain:
Brigham

Being that this is a distance sampling forum, I feel obliged to note that making comparisons between encounter rates is effectively contrasting counts, with counts adjusted for transect length.  Such comparisons make no allowance for changes in detectability.  It is easy to imagine a scenario in which animal density differed considerably between two times/locations, but encounter rates were indistinguishable; because changes in detectability counter-acted the difference in density.

In other words, differences in encounter rates don't tell you much about differences in density.  You need measurements of detection probability to complete the picture.  Hence, that's why you find little information about comparing encounter rates.

John

Not exactly trivial.  Here's some poorly documented R code working with the online crabeater seal data.

It performs the log(group size) vs Pr(detection) regression.  Then it performs back-calculation to derive a point estimate of expected group size when detection probability=1.

However, the hard part is producing a measure of precision for that point estimate.  You need a measure of precision (a variance) so that you can propagate the uncertainty of the detection function, encounter rate AND expected group size to produce overall uncertainty in your estimate of abundance.

I've take an easy case here, with a half-normal detection function model without adjustment terms.  If you had a more complex model, you would need more sophistication in the computation of sigma and phats.

library(Distance)
seals <- read.csv(file = MailScanner has detected a possible fraud attempt from "distancesampling.org" claiming to be "http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/crabbieMCDS.csv" <http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/crabbieMCDS.csv>)
halfnorm <- ds(seals, adjustment = NULL)
plot(halfnorm)
table(seals$size)  # not a good example because there is little variation in school size
sigma <- exp(halfnorm$ddf$par[1])
phats <- exp(-seals$distance^2/(2 * sigma^2))
log.schools <- log(seals$size)
size.regr <- lm(log.schools ~ phats)
my.value <- data.frame(phats=c(1))
log.expected.school.size <- predict(size.regr, se.fit = TRUE, newdata = my.value)
expected.school.size <- exp(log.expected.school.size$fit)
term1.for.var <- log.expected.school.size$se.fit^2
var.expected.school.size <- expected.school.size^2 * term1.for.var
se.expected.school.size <- sqrt(var.expected.school.size)

On 10/12/2017 22:39, Valentina Zini wrote:

"Stabilize" in the sense that if the EDF is close to k, I would double k
and see if there is a big change in the EDF in the refitted model.

> 2) I was reading choose.k from mgcv package.
> "A useful general purpose approach goes as follows: (i) fit your model
> and extract the deviance residuals; (ii) for each smooth term in your
> model, fit an equivalent, single, smooth to the residuals, using a
> substantially increased k to see if there is a pattern in the residuals
> that could potentially be explained by increasing k". I am doing this
> but I am first fitting the model without the smoothed parameter. The
> residuals have a huge amount of zeros, so I would use a Tweedie response
> distribution. I also use a Tweedie in the first model. The obvious issue
> is that being residuals they are not positive.
> What response distribution should I choose to fit the residuals? Should
> I transform them?

Indeed, Tweedie is a good choice for most DSMs. For fitting to the
residuals, the deviance residuals should be normally distributed if the
model is correct (see, e.g., p. 113 of Wood, 2017 or any other text on
GLMs/GAMs). Therefore no transformation is necessary.

Hope this helps.

cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Don, hi listfolk,

Rather than jumping into either approach, if you simple want the dots to
be colour-coded, you can do something along the lines of the code below
(using the golf tee data shipped with mrds).

We don't have code to do this in general in Distance or mrds because
it's relly tricky once you have multiple continuous covariates in the
model. You can customise the below if you have continuous covariates by
using the quantile() function, storing the results in a column of
plotdat and then subsetting based on that.

Hopefully a forthcoming version of mrds will have a better solution,
when I can think of one.

Hope this helps in the meantime!

cheers,
--dave

---

library(mrds)
data(book.tee.data)
# fit to only observer 1 data
egdata <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe
egdata <- egdata[egdata$observer==1, ]

# fit model with sex and exposure as covariates
result <- ddf(dsmodel = ~mcds(key = "hn", formula = ~sex+exposure),
               data = egdata, method = "ds")

# don't plot the points
plot(result, showpoints=FALSE)

# get the data used in the model
plotdat <- result$data

# get the probabilities of detection **at a given distance** and
# store in a column of plotdat
plotdat$p <- detfct(plotdat$distance, ddfobj=result$ds$aux$ddfobj,
                     width=result$ds$aux$width)

## plot over the different combinations in the data
# sex=1, exposure=1
points(plotdat$distance[plotdat$sex==1 & plotdat$exposure==1],
        plotdat$p[plotdat$sex==1 & plotdat$exposure==1], col="red")

# sex=0, exposure=1
points(plotdat$distance[plotdat$sex==0 & plotdat$exposure==1],
        plotdat$p[plotdat$sex==0 & plotdat$exposure==1], col="green")

# sex=0, exposure=0
points(plotdat$distance[plotdat$sex==0 & plotdat$exposure==0],
        plotdat$p[plotdat$sex==0 & plotdat$exposure==0], col="pink")

# sex=1, exposure=0
points(plotdat$distance[plotdat$sex==1 & plotdat$exposure==0],
        plotdat$p[plotdat$sex==1 & plotdat$exposure==0], col="blue")

# make a legend
legend(2.5, 1.2, c("sex=1, exposure=1", "sex=0, exposure=1",
                    "sex=0, exposure=0","sex=1, exposure=0"),
        c("red", "green", "pink", "blue"))
